paper.title: Competing Demographic Drivers of Hospital Expenditures: Coexistence of the Red Herring and the Steepening Effects
paper.code_data_availability: Data Availability Statement (p. 942): 'The data used for this analysis are available upon submission of an application to Statistics Denmark, https://www.dst.dk/en. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish register data from Statistics Denmark (Statistics Denmark 2023)
the deaths register (DODAASG) (Danish Health Data Authority 2024)
the DRG registers / Diagnosis-Related Grouping (DRG) tariffs calculated by the Danish Health Data Authority (Statens Serum Institut 2014)

linkages: Each interaction with a hospital is associated with a pseudonymized person identifier, allowing hospital services to be attributed to individual patients
Time-to-death is constructed by linking the date of birth from the population register (BEF) to the date of death from the deaths register (DODAASG)

sample.universe: The entire Danish population, with the analysis focused on individuals aged 30 and older; register data cover 2002-2022 and hospital expenditures 2002-2017
sample.unit_of_observation: person-month (monthly somatic hospital expenditures per individual)
selection_rules: All individuals in the Danish population registers are included
Focus on those aged 30 and older, in line with existing literature
Hospital expenditures observed 2002-2017; analysis of hospital services restricted to the period prior to 2018 because of substantial changes in the hospital registers in 2018

Time-to-death determined precisely for all individuals within the four years preceding death; for individuals alive beyond 2021 time-to-death is right-censored, set to four years with a binary censoring indicator equal to one
Table 1 and Table 2 models estimated on a random subsample of 10,000,000 monthly observations, of which 2,191,490 enter the Poisson (intensive margin) part
Tables 3 and 4 estimate the Joint Model separately by age-sex group and by time-to-death-sex group
Table 5 uses the entire Danish population in 2002 and 2017, with monthly expenditures aggregated to annual amounts
sample.n_observations: 638,184,716 monthly observations after combining the registers; 109,381,459 individual hospital interactions recorded 2002-2017

construction_notes: Hospital expenditures are DRG tariffs calculated by the Danish Health Data Authority at a highly detailed procedure-specific level; they account for variable costs (staff time, equipment, most specialized pharmaceuticals) but not fixed costs, and include additional costs when a stay extends beyond the standard treatment duration
Expenditures are aggregated into monthly amounts capturing all expenditures incurred from the first to the last day of each month; stays spanning several months are distributed proportionally by days
Expenditures are inflated to 2020 levels in DKK with the Statistics Denmark consumer price index and converted to 2020 USD at the 2020 exchange rate of 1/6.534 (Danmarks Nationalbank 2024)
Both age and time-to-death are measured in years, with decimal values representing additional days
Calendar time is measured in years at a monthly resolution as (year - 2002) + (month - 1)/12, setting January 1, 2002 as the base date
Time-to-death is set to four and the binary censoring indicator to one if an individual has not died through the period of observation
Age*Time is divided by 100 in the Probit and Poisson regressions but not in E_psi, to ensure convergence in the numerical optimization

Government insurance covers nearly all hospital procedures in Denmark: out-of-pocket expenses account for 4.6% and private health insurance for 0.9% of total hospital expenditures; somatic hospital expenditures were 47% of total publicly funded healthcare expenditures in Denmark in 2017
In the decomposition, ages are integers from 30 to 110+ and time-to-death is rounded to the first decimal
Aggregate annual expenditures were checked against the raw DRG register data and against age-specific averages in B. J. Christensen et al. (2016) and Kollerup et al. (2022)

claims.statement: In the Naïve parametrization of the two-part model estimated on the whole Danish population aged 30+, age is positively associated with the probability of incurring positive monthly somatic hospital expenditures (Probit column).

register_source.value: BEF (population register): date of birth

definition.value: Individual age, measured in years with decimal values representing additional days, entered linearly in the index functions X'_i delta and X'_i gamma of the two-part model; the sample is restricted to individuals aged 30 and above.

timing.value: Measured at each monthly observation over 2002-2017

outcome.label: Indicator for positive monthly somatic hospital expenditures (extensive margin)

register_source.value: DRG registers (Diagnosis-Related Grouping tariffs, Danish Health Data Authority), accessed via Statistics Denmark

definition.value: First part of the two-part model: Pr(H_i > 0 | X_i) = F(X'_i delta), the probability that an individual incurs positive somatic hospital expenditures in a given month, estimated with a Probit specification. Hospital expenditures are DRG (Diagnosis-Related Grouping) tariffs calculated by the Danish Health Data Authority at a procedure-specific level, aggregated to monthly amounts covering all expenditures incurred from the first to the last day of each month, inflated to 2020 DKK with the Statistics Denmark consumer price index and converted to 2020 USD at the 2020 exchange rate of 1/6.534.

timing.value: Monthly, 2002-2017

units.value: probit index points per year of age

estimand.target_population: the entire Danish population aged 30 and above over 2002-2017 (average marginal association over the estimation sample)

population.description: The entire Danish population aged 30 and above, monthly observations 2002-2017; the models are estimated on a random subsample of 10,000,000 monthly observations, of which 2,191,490 enter the Poisson part.
population.selection: All individuals in the Danish population registers aged 30 and above; hospital services restricted to the period prior to 2018 because of substantial changes in the hospital registers in 2018; a random subsample of 10,000,000 monthly observations is drawn for computational reasons.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. The paper estimates marginal associations between age, time-to-death, calendar time and their interaction and monthly somatic hospital expenditures in observational population register data; the exhibits are labelled 'marginal association' and the authors state that the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death remains largely unexamined.

key_assumptions.assumption: Correct specification of the conditional mean function: quasi-maximum likelihood with robust standard errors gives consistent parameter estimates and valid inference even under distributional misspecification, so only the conditional mean need be correctly specified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Endnote 1 states robustness estimates are conducted against the conditional mean function specification; an expanded parametrization is reported in Online Appendix C.1

key_assumptions.assumption: Time-to-death is treated as a regressor that is exogenous to hospital expenditures: the model contains no channel running from hospital expenditures to time-to-death. The authors describe this endogeneity as a longstanding concern that potentially influences their analysis and leave it unresolved.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the authors discuss the concern, note that others have used instrumental variables or predetermined-expenditure approaches, and state that the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death remains largely unexamined

key_assumptions.assumption: Health status, morbidity and income are omitted from the model although the authors acknowledge their potential impact on the aging-expenditure relationship and report that prior research finds the Red Herring effect to be mediated by health status.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the authors argue these factors are beyond the scope of the Red Herring and Steepening Hypotheses as defined in the literature

key_assumptions.assumption: Censoring convention: time-to-death is set to four years and the binary indicator X-check* to one when an individual has not died through the period of observation, so right-censored survivors enter the regression at a fixed time-to-death value.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors cite Seshamani and Gray (2004b), who find time-to-death effects on hospital expenditures become negligible beyond four years

key_assumptions.assumption: Clustering at the individual level with a cluster-robust variance estimator (Liang and Zeger 1986) properly captures the dependencies in the data.
Estimates obtained on a random subsample of 10,000,000 monthly observations (2,191,490 of which enter the Poisson part) represent the full set of 638,184,716 monthly observations.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The subsample is stated to be random and is imposed by computational resources; no comparison with the full sample is reported

threats_discussed: plausible endogeneity between hospital expenditures and time-to-death (Salas and Raftery 2001): if hospital services prolong life, higher expenditures may be both a consequence and a cause of longer time-to-death
right-censoring of time-to-death for individuals alive beyond 2021
with 638M observations (10M in the regression subsamples) conventional significance thresholds may identify statistically significant effects that are economically negligible
omission of health status and income, which prior research suggests mediate the Red Herring effect
changes in the hospital registers in 2018, which is why hospital services are restricted to before 2018
robustness_checks: Bayesian hypothesis tests with Bayes factors and Bayesian p-values (Kass and Raftery 1995), robust to priors from Pr(H0) = 0.01 to Pr(H0) = 0.99

expanded model parametrization (Online Appendix C.1)
separate estimation for the female and male populations (Online Appendix C.3)
aggregate annual expenditures validated against the raw DRG register data and against age-specific averages in B. J. Christensen et al. (2016) and Kollerup et al. (2022)

definition.value: Years remaining until the individual's death, measured in years with decimal values representing additional days, constructed from the date of birth in the population register (BEF) and the date of death in the deaths register (DODAASG, covering deaths through the end of 2022); in practice time-to-death is set to four and the binary censoring indicator X-check* to one for individuals not observed to die within the observation window.

timing.value: Measured at each monthly observation over 2002-2017, looking forward to the date of death

outcome.label: Monthly somatic hospital expenditures in 2020 USD conditional on being positive (intensive margin)

register_source.value: DRG registers (Diagnosis-Related Grouping tariffs, Danish Health Data Authority), accessed via Statistics Denmark

definition.value: Second part of the two-part model: the distribution of positive monthly somatic hospital expenditures, H_i | X_i, H_i > 0, modelled as g(X'_i gamma) with a Poisson-distributed generalized linear model with a log link. Hospital expenditures are DRG (Diagnosis-Related Grouping) tariffs calculated by the Danish Health Data Authority at a procedure-specific level, aggregated to monthly amounts covering all expenditures incurred from the first to the last day of each month, inflated to 2020 DKK with the Statistics Denmark consumer price index and converted to 2020 USD at the 2020 exchange rate of 1/6.534.

timing.value: Monthly, 2002-2017

units.value: log points of monthly somatic hospital expenditure per additional year of time-to-death

estimand.target_population: the entire Danish population aged 30 and above over 2002-2017 (average marginal association over the estimation sample)

population.description: The entire Danish population aged 30 and above, monthly observations 2002-2017; the models are estimated on a random subsample of 10,000,000 monthly observations, of which 2,191,490 enter the Poisson part.
population.selection: All individuals in the Danish population registers aged 30 and above; hospital services restricted to the period prior to 2018 because of substantial changes in the hospital registers in 2018; a random subsample of 10,000,000 monthly observations is drawn for computational reasons.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. The paper estimates marginal associations between age, time-to-death, calendar time and their interaction and monthly somatic hospital expenditures in observational population register data; the exhibits are labelled 'marginal association' and the authors state that the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death remains largely unexamined.

key_assumptions.assumption: Correct specification of the conditional mean function: quasi-maximum likelihood with robust standard errors gives consistent parameter estimates and valid inference even under distributional misspecification, so only the conditional mean need be correctly specified.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Endnote 1 states robustness estimates are conducted against the conditional mean function specification; an expanded parametrization is reported in Online Appendix C.1

key_assumptions.assumption: Time-to-death is treated as a regressor that is exogenous to hospital expenditures: the model contains no channel running from hospital expenditures to time-to-death. The authors describe this endogeneity as a longstanding concern that potentially influences their analysis and leave it unresolved.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the authors discuss the concern, note that others have used instrumental variables or predetermined-expenditure approaches, and state that the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death remains largely unexamined

key_assumptions.assumption: Health status, morbidity and income are omitted from the model although the authors acknowledge their potential impact on the aging-expenditure relationship and report that prior research finds the Red Herring effect to be mediated by health status.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the authors argue these factors are beyond the scope of the Red Herring and Steepening Hypotheses as defined in the literature

key_assumptions.assumption: Censoring convention: time-to-death is set to four years and the binary indicator X-check* to one when an individual has not died through the period of observation, so right-censored survivors enter the regression at a fixed time-to-death value.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors cite Seshamani and Gray (2004b), who find time-to-death effects on hospital expenditures become negligible beyond four years

key_assumptions.assumption: Clustering at the individual level with a cluster-robust variance estimator (Liang and Zeger 1986) properly captures the dependencies in the data.
Estimates obtained on a random subsample of 10,000,000 monthly observations (2,191,490 of which enter the Poisson part) represent the full set of 638,184,716 monthly observations.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The subsample is stated to be random and is imposed by computational resources; no comparison with the full sample is reported

threats_discussed: plausible endogeneity between hospital expenditures and time-to-death (Salas and Raftery 2001): if hospital services prolong life, higher expenditures may be both a consequence and a cause of longer time-to-death
right-censoring of time-to-death for individuals alive beyond 2021
with 638M observations (10M in the regression subsamples) conventional significance thresholds may identify statistically significant effects that are economically negligible
omission of health status and income, which prior research suggests mediate the Red Herring effect
changes in the hospital registers in 2018, which is why hospital services are restricted to before 2018
robustness_checks: Bayesian hypothesis tests with Bayes factors and Bayesian p-values (Kass and Raftery 1995), robust to priors from Pr(H0) = 0.01 to Pr(H0) = 0.99
Wald tests on the average marginal effects as well as on the parameters (Online Appendix B.2)
expanded model parametrization (Online Appendix C.1)
separate estimation for the female and male populations (Online Appendix C.3)
aggregate annual expenditures validated against the raw DRG register data and against age-specific averages in B. J. Christensen et al. (2016) and Kollerup et al. (2022)
decomposition recomputed for t1 = 2015 and t2 = 2005 (Online Appendix C.6)
unresolved_confounders: the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death, which the authors say remains largely unexamined in this literature
health status / morbidity, which prior research suggests mediates the Red Herring effect and which Carreras et al. (2018) find renders time-to-death statistically insignificant

estimation.specification: Two-part model of Equation (1) with the Red Herring linear parametrization of Equation (3)
estimation.clustering: individual level (cluster-robust variance estimator, Liang and Zeger 1986)

sample_n.value: 10,000,000 monthly observations; 2,191,490 observations in the Poisson part

source_table.value: Table 1, Red Herring panel, Poisson column, row TTD

mediators_claimed: health status / morbidity (prior research suggests the Red Herring effect is mediated by health status; not included in this paper's model)

heterogeneity.finding: Table 3 re-estimates the Joint Model separately by 10-year age group and sex; time-to-death effects generally increase in absolute magnitude across age groups and Steepening effects are most pronounced between ages 50 and 80, while males generally exhibit higher time-to-death and Steepening effects than females.

Table 4 re-estimates the Joint Model separately by time-to-death group and sex; time-to-death effects are far larger for person-months within 1.5 years of death, and Steepening is negative for females closest to death but large and positive for males.

heterogeneity.finding: The magnitude of the effects differ by sex and are statistically significantly different from each other (Online Appendix C.4, Table A16), with males generally exhibiting higher time-to-death and Steepening effects than females.

Time-to-death and Steepening effects are generally statistically different across age groups as implied by Welch tests (Online Appendix C.4, Table A15); time-to-death effects generally increase in absolute magnitude with age, Steepening is most pronounced between ages 50 and 80 and negative for females aged 30-40 and for both sexes aged 90+.

Replicated by margin in Online Appendix C.4, Table A12: the extensive margin shows positive Steepening across nearly all groups (except females 90+), while the intensive margin shows slower growth for ages 30-40 and 80+, particularly for males 90+ (-$26.41).

The paper estimates marginal associations between age, time-to-death, calendar time and their interaction and monthly somatic hospital expenditures in observational population register data; the exhibits are labelled 'marginal association' and the authors state that the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death remains largely unexamined.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. The paper estimates marginal associations between age, time-to-death, calendar time and their interaction and monthly somatic hospital expenditures in observational population register data; the exhibits are labelled 'marginal association' and the authors state that the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death remains largely unexamined.

key_assumptions.assumption: Time-to-death is treated as a regressor that is exogenous to hospital expenditures: the model contains no channel running from hospital expenditures to time-to-death. heterogeneity.finding: The magnitude of the effects differ by sex and are statistically significantly different from each other (Online Appendix C.4, Table A16), with males generally exhibiting higher time-to-death and Steepening effects than females.

Time-to-death and Steepening effects are generally statistically different across age groups as implied by Welch tests (Online Appendix C.4, Table A15); time-to-death effects generally increase in absolute magnitude with age, Steepening is most pronounced between ages 50 and 80 and negative for females aged 30-40 and for both sexes aged 90+.

Replicated by margin in Online Appendix C.4, Table A12: the extensive margin shows positive Steepening across nearly all groups (except females 90+), while the intensive margin shows slower growth for ages 30-40 and 80+, particularly for males 90+ (-$26.41).

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. The paper estimates marginal associations between age, time-to-death, calendar time and their interaction and monthly somatic hospital expenditures in observational population register data; the exhibits are labelled 'marginal association' and the authors state that the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death remains largely unexamined.

key_assumptions.assumption: Time-to-death is treated as a regressor that is exogenous to hospital expenditures: the model contains no channel running from hospital expenditures to time-to-death. key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the authors discuss the concern, note that others have used instrumental variables or predetermined-expenditure approaches, and state that the direct causal effect of hospital expenditures on time-to-death remains largely unexamined

key_assumptions.assumption: Health status, morbidity and income are omitted from the model although the authors acknowledge their potential impact on the aging-expenditure relationship and report that prior research finds the Red Herring effect to be mediated by health status.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None offered; the authors argue these factors are beyond the scope of the Red Herring and Steepening Hypotheses as defined in the literature

The Steepening effects differ significantly between females and males for each time-to-death group (Online Appendix C.5, Table A19); males exhibit a substantially larger degree of Steepening in all three groups ($40.06, $14.74 and $8.11 versus -$5.84, $3.88 and $6.92).

Online Appendix C.5, Table A17: at the extensive margin all subgroups show positive Steepening; at the intensive margin Steepening is negative for both sexes with 1.5-4 years to death and for females with < 1.5 years (-$13.09), while males with < 1.5 years are an exception ($14.73) and groups with > 4 years to death show insignificant intensive-margin Steepening.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation: an accounting decomposition of the observed 2002-2017 difference in aggregate annual somatic hospital expenditures into population-structure and expenditure-level components, similar in spirit to the Kitagawa (1955) and Oaxaca (1973)-Blinder (1973) decompositions.

key_assumptions.assumption: Annual aggregate hospital expenditures can be written as the sum over age and time-to-death groups of group size times group mean expenditure; the authors state this formulation relies on directly observable data without imposing restrictive functional assumptions on the relationships between expenditures, age, time-to-death or calendar time.

The counterfactual defining the Red Herring Error term holds the age-specific near-death expenditure gap fixed at its t1 (2017) level: the underestimation term remains time-invariant at the t1 level, signifying that the Red Herring hypothesis addresses the relationship between age and time-to-death without making statements about intertemporal changes.

The decomposition is an accounting identity evaluated at a particular weighting - t1 (2017) mean expenditures for the population-change terms and t2 (2002) population counts for the expenditure-change terms - so the split between components depends on that choice.

The sum of the Red Herring Error term and the Red Herring-Steepening term must be zero (proved in Appendix A.1), so the two components are necessarily equal in magnitude and opposite in sign rather than independently estimated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Proof in Appendix A.1

threats_discussed: the Steepening component also absorbs broader time trends, including underlying technology, and so is not a pure age-time interaction
the estimates reflect the particular 2002-2017 window and should not be interpreted as universal constants

unresolved_confounders: technological advancement, multimorbidity, and shifts in hospital utilization and prices, which the Discussion lists as possible mechanisms behind the Steepening component but does not separate

key_assumptions.assumption: Annual aggregate hospital expenditures can be written as the sum over age and time-to-death groups of group size times group mean expenditure; the authors state this formulation relies on directly observable data without imposing restrictive functional assumptions on the relationships between expenditures, age, time-to-death or calendar time.

The counterfactual defining the Red Herring Error term holds the age-specific near-death expenditure gap fixed at its t1 (2017) level: the underestimation term remains time-invariant at the t1 level, signifying that the Red Herring hypothesis addresses the relationship between age and time-to-death without making statements about intertemporal changes.

The decomposition is an accounting identity evaluated at a particular weighting - t1 (2017) mean expenditures for the population-change terms and t2 (2002) population counts for the expenditure-change terms - so the split between components depends on that choice.

The sum of the Red Herring Error term and the Red Herring-Steepening term must be zero (proved in Appendix A.1), so the two components are necessarily equal in magnitude and opposite in sign rather than independently estimated.
